name: Policy Framing for Resilience
consequences: Reframing digital identity as a resilience imperative rather than a privacy issue shifts institutional priorities toward contingency planning. This risks diluting technical specificity in favor of broad policy language, potentially weakening enforceable requirements.
options: Anchor policy proposals in national security frameworks to mandate fallback authentication paths for critical infrastructure
Leverage EU-wide digital resilience directives to pressure Danish regulators into adopting platform-neutral standards
Position fallback mechanisms as a public-utility obligation similar to power-grid redundancy requirements
review: Prioritizing resilience framing risks abstracting technical details, leaving implementation specifics unaddressed without explicit procurement mandates.

name: Technical Demonstrators as Credibility Anchors
consequences: Building non-production demonstrators creates tangible evidence of platform-neutral alternatives but risks being dismissed as academic exercises without institutional buy-in. This could delay real-world testing until after critical procurement decisions are locked in.
options: Develop a FIDO2/WebAuthn-based authentication flow for GrapheneOS that bypasses platform integrity APIs entirely
Create a browser-based authentication prototype using decentralized identifiers and open-source trust frameworks
Build a hardware-token fallback system requiring no mobile OS integration for high-assurance use cases
review: Demonstrators may lack production-grade security certifications, creating a gap in proving real-world viability without formal testing environments.

name: Coalition Diversification
consequences: Expanding stakeholder engagement beyond traditional digital governance circles strengthens political pressure but risks fragmenting focus across competing priorities like privacy, security, and accessibility.
options: Form an industry-academia-government consortium to co-develop open standards for platform-neutral authentication
Engage civil society organizations to frame fallback mechanisms as democratic accountability tools
Partner with Nordic digital sovereignty groups to create cross-border advocacy pressure
review: Diversifying coalitions may dilute technical expertise, leaving gaps in addressing specific implementation challenges without dedicated engineering support.

name: Procurement Language Standardization
consequences: Influencing procurement requirements to mandate platform neutrality creates enforceable change but faces resistance from vendors and agencies invested in existing ecosystems. This could slow adoption if requirements lack technical precision.
options: Insert explicit platform-neutral authentication clauses into AltID's procurement specifications for public-sector integration
Require all digital identity solutions to demonstrate fallback-path compatibility during certification processes
Develop a standardized evaluation framework for assessing supplier concentration risks in identity infrastructure
review: Standardization efforts may lack enforcement mechanisms, leaving gaps in ensuring compliance without institutional oversight.

name: EU Alignment Strategy
consequences: Tying Danish advocacy to European Digital Identity Wallet frameworks amplifies influence but risks subordinating national priorities to broader EU agendas. This could delay localized solutions if European standards prioritize different technical approaches.
options: Propose platform-neutral authentication requirements as a contribution to the European Digital Identity Wallet's resilience guidelines
Leverage EU interoperability mandates to pressure member states into adopting fallback-path standards
Create a Nordic EU advocacy group to coordinate regional digital sovereignty priorities
review: EU alignment may prioritize harmonization over localized resilience needs, leaving gaps in addressing Denmark-specific operational requirements.

name: Regulatory Sandboxing for Fallback Mechanisms
consequences: Establishing regulatory sandboxes for testing fallback authentication paths enables controlled experimentation but requires navigating complex compliance landscapes. This could delay deployment if regulatory approval processes are slow.
options: Create a restricted testing environment for hardware-token authentication under NSIS security classifications
Develop a phased rollout plan for fallback mechanisms in low-risk public services before high-assurance applications
Partner with financial regulators to test platform-neutral authentication in banking sector pilot programs
review: Sandboxing may lack scalability, creating a gap between controlled testing environments and real-world deployment challenges.

name: Certification Pathway Diversification
consequences: Expanding certification criteria beyond Apple/Google platform signals could weaken existing trust frameworks, forcing re-evaluation of what constitutes 'secure' authentication. This risks delaying adoption if alternative certifications lack institutional credibility.
options: Establish a public-sector-validated certification body for platform-neutral authentication methods
Integrate third-party security audits into existing eIDAS compliance workflows
Create a dual-track certification process allowing legacy platform signals alongside open-standard alternatives
review: Diversifying certification pathways risks fragmenting trust metrics, leaving gaps in interoperability between legacy and alternative systems without explicit compatibility mandates.

name: Alternative Authentication Ecosystems
consequences: Prioritizing hardware tokens or decentralized identifiers could improve resilience but may reduce user adoption due to perceived complexity. This shifts reliance from platform vendors to hardware manufacturers and protocol standards.
options: Develop a national hardware token program with open-source firmware for public-sector use
Pilot blockchain-based identity verification for non-critical services to build institutional familiarity
Create a mandatory dual-factor requirement combining platform signals with biometric verification
review: Focusing on alternative ecosystems creates a dependency on new infrastructure providers, leaving unaddressed how to transition legacy systems without service disruptions.

name: Stakeholder Incentive Realignment
consequences: Revising procurement incentives to prioritize platform neutrality could pressure vendors to adapt, but may face resistance from incumbents. This shifts risk management responsibilities to private-sector partners.
options: Tie public-sector contracts to compliance with platform-neutral authentication standards
Implement a risk-sharing model where vendors contribute to fallback infrastructure development
Create a public-private innovation fund for alternative authentication research and deployment
review: Realigning incentives risks creating new power imbalances between state and private actors, leaving unaddressed how to maintain oversight of emerging authentication providers.

name: Interoperability Layer Standardization
consequences: Mandating open standards for identity verification could break platform monopolies but requires overcoming entrenched technical and regulatory barriers. This shifts complexity from end-users to system integrators.
options: Require all public-sector identity systems to use open-source authentication protocol stacks
Create a national API interoperability framework for cross-platform identity verification
Standardize on FIDO2-compliant hardware tokens for critical services
review: Standardizing interoperability layers risks creating new technical debt if legacy systems cannot adapt, leaving gaps in service continuity during transition periods.

name: Public-Private Resilience Partnerships
consequences: Collaborating with private-sector stakeholders to build fallback infrastructure could accelerate adoption but may dilute public control over digital identity systems. This introduces new accountability challenges.
options: Form a joint public-private task force to design and test fallback authentication scenarios
Require private-sector identity providers to contribute resources to national fallback infrastructure
Establish a shared risk-mitigation fund for platform-related service disruptions
review: Public-private partnerships risk prioritizing commercial interests over public good, leaving unaddressed how to enforce accountability for critical infrastructure failures.

name: Decentralized Trust Architecture
consequences: Shifting to decentralized trust models reduces reliance on centralized platform vendors, but requires redefining existing certification hierarchies. This could delay integration with legacy public-sector systems that depend on established OS trust roots.
options: Implement blockchain-based identity verification protocols to bypass centralized OS dependencies
Develop open-source authentication frameworks compatible with multiple OS environments
Partner with local tech firms to create alternative OS-independent authentication services
review: Decentralizing trust architecture shifts reliance from OS vendors but risks regulatory non-compliance and underdeveloped ecosystem support

name: Cross-Platform Compatibility Mandates
consequences: Enforcing compatibility across platforms streamlines access but may slow innovation cycles. This creates friction with platform-specific security updates and feature rollouts.
options: Require all public-sector apps to support WebAuthn across iOS, Android, and desktop platforms
Advocate for mandatory OS-agnostic authentication modules in Danish procurement contracts
Establish a certification process for third-party authentication tools that meet eIDAS2 resilience criteria
review: Mandating cross-platform compatibility ensures broader access but may stifle platform-specific innovations and face procurement resistance

name: Localized Authentication Infrastructure
consequences: Building local infrastructure enhances sovereignty but increases operational complexity. This creates dependency on domestic technical expertise that may not yet exist at scale.
options: Deploy regional identity verification servers under Danish jurisdiction to reduce foreign data transit
Create a national open-source authentication library to replace proprietary OS components
Collaborate with Danish cloud providers to host fallback authentication services domestically
review: Localizing infrastructure boosts sovereignty but increases operational costs and may lack the scale of global providers

name: Public-Private Authentication Partnerships
consequences: Encouraging private sector involvement diversifies resources but introduces conflicting priorities. This risks diluting public-interest objectives through commercial constraints.
options: Form alliances with Danish banks to co-develop platform-neutral authentication standards
Engage telecom providers in creating alternative verification channels outside OS ecosystems
Establish joint working groups with private sector tech firms to explore non-platform-dependent solutions
review: Public-private partnerships diversify resources but risk prioritizing commercial interests over public resilience needs

name: Regulatory Contingency Frameworks
consequences: Creating contingency protocols institutionalizes resilience planning but requires political buy-in. This may not address immediate technical limitations in fallback systems.
options: Draft emergency protocols for identity access if Apple/Google services become unavailable
Push for legal mandates requiring fallback authentication in all public-sector digital contracts
Develop a regulatory sandbox for testing alternative authentication methods under controlled conditions
review: Regulatory contingency frameworks provide preparedness but depend on political will and may lack immediate enforcement mechanisms

name: User-Centric Authentication Design
consequences: Prioritizing user control over platform-specific features could increase adoption but may conflict with existing security architectures. This creates tension between usability and compliance requirements.
options: Design authentication interfaces that prioritize user control over platform-specific features
Conduct user studies to identify non-platform-dependent authentication preferences
Integrate multi-factor authentication options that bypass OS-centric verification flows
review: User-centric design enhances accessibility but may conflict with existing platform security protocols and technical limitations

name: International Standards Advocacy
consequences: Aligning with global standards strengthens credibility but may dilute national-specific resilience priorities. This creates dependency on external regulatory timelines.
options: Lobby EU standards bodies to include platform-neutral authentication in digital identity guidelines
Participate in global identity forums to promote alternative authentication models
Align Danish proposals with international resilience benchmarks for digital identity systems
review: Advocating international standards leverages broader support but may compromise tailored national resilience strategies
